message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
Internal Audit Memo: Missed Appointments in Outpatient Physiotherapy
To: Director of Operations, Therapies Division
From: Clinical Audit Team
Date: 14 August 2026

1. Scope
This audit examined missed appointments in the outpatient physiotherapy service across our three clinic sites between 1 January and 30 June 2026. For the purposes of this audit, a "did not attend" (DNA) is recorded when a patient fails to attend without giving notice. Late cancellations (less than 24 hours' notice) are recorded and reported separately, because the slot can sometimes be offered to another patient. We reviewed the appointment system records for all 24,860 booked appointments in the period and interviewed reception and clinical staff at each site.

2. Overall position
There were 2,610 DNAs in the period, a DNA rate of 10.5%, against the service target of 8%. Each DNA leaves a 30-minute clinical slot unused. At the service's average cost per clinical hour of £62, the 1,305 lost clinical hours represent around £80,900 of clinical time over six months.

Table 1. DNA rate by appointment type
Appointment type | Booked | DNAs | DNA rate
New patient assessment | 6,210 | 410 | 6.6%
Follow-up | 18,650 | 2,200 | 11.8%
Total | 24,860 | 2,610 | 10.5%

Follow-up appointments account for most DNAs. Staff told us that many patients stop attending once their symptoms improve, without telling the service.

3. Reminder calls
Since 2024, reception staff have phoned patients two working days before their appointment where time allows. In the audit period, staff made reminder calls for 7,800 appointments, about 300 a week over the 26 weeks. A call is recorded as received only if the patient answered and confirmed they would attend; unanswered calls are not recorded. Reception staff estimate that each call, including dialling, rescheduling where needed and updating the record, takes an average of four minutes.

Table 2. DNA rate by reminder status
Reminder status | Appointments | DNAs | DNA rate
Reminder call received | 7,800 | 470 | 6.0%
No reminder call recorded | 17,060 | 2,140 | 12.5%

Patients who received a reminder call were less than half as likely to miss their appointment. Reminder calls therefore more than halve the DNA rate, and extending them to all appointments would bring the service well within its 8% target.

4. Discharge policy
The service's policy is that a patient who DNAs twice without explanation is discharged back to their referrer. We found the policy was applied inconsistently: of 160 patients who met the criterion, 104 were discharged. Staff were reluctant to discharge patients they knew to be vulnerable.

5. Late cancellations
In addition to the DNAs above, 1,140 appointments were cancelled with less than 24 hours' notice. Reception staff were able to refill 31% of these slots, usually with patients on the cancellation list.

6. Findings and recommendations
Finding 1. The DNA rate of 10.5% (including late cancellations, which we classify as DNAs) is above target and costs the service around £80,900 in clinical time every six months.
Recommendation 1. Extend reminder calls to all booked appointments, about 960 a week, using reception staff. This can be absorbed within existing reception hours at no additional cost.

Finding 2. The two-DNA discharge policy is applied inconsistently.
Recommendation 2. Revise the policy to include a documented clinical review before discharge, so that vulnerable patients are protected and the policy can then be applied consistently.

Finding 3. Late-cancellation slots are refilled only 31% of the time.
Recommendation 3. Introduce an automated text offer to patients on the cancellation list when a slot becomes free.

7. Conclusion
Missed appointments are costly but largely preventable. Reminder calls have been shown to more than halve DNAs in this service, and extending them to every patient, together with the policy and process changes above, should bring the DNA rate below target within six months.
</document>
response:
# Review of the audit memo

The arithmetic mostly checks out, but the memo's central causal claim and its "no additional cost" claim are not supported by its own data. Those two problems carry Recommendation 1 and the conclusion.

## Major issues

**1. The reminder-call effect is presented as causal, but the data can't show that.**
- Table 2 is correct: 470/7,800 = 6.0% and 2,140/17,060 = 12.5%. But it compares two groups that were not assigned at random.
- A call counts as "received" only if the patient answered and confirmed they would attend. Anyone who didn't answer, or who said they wouldn't come, falls into the "no reminder" group. That group is therefore loaded with likely DNAs by construction, while the "received" group is pre-filtered for engaged patients.
- Calls were made "where time allows", so staff discretion likely played a part in who was called.
- The two groups may also differ in appointment type. Table 1 shows follow-ups DNA at 11.8% against 6.6% for new assessments.
- "Reminder calls therefore more than halve the DNA rate" and "have been shown to more than halve DNAs" are overstated. Even taken at face value, 6.0/12.5 = 0.48, which is only just under half.
- The claim that extending calls "would bring the service well within its 8% target" assumes the 6% rate would carry over to patients who don't answer or who are less engaged. This is unsupported.

**2. "Absorbed within existing reception hours at no additional cost" contradicts the memo's own figures.**
- At 4 minutes per call, the 7,800 calls took about 520 hours over 26 weeks, or 20 hours a week.
- Calling all 24,860 appointments would take about 1,657 hours, or about 64 hours a week. That is roughly 44 extra hours a week, more than a full-time post.
- Unanswered calls aren't recorded, so the true number of dial attempts and the true time are higher still.
- The memo says calls happen only "where time allows", which suggests reception has no spare capacity. Recommendation 1 needs a costed workload estimate. An automated text or call system, which Recommendation 3 already proposes for cancellations, might be cheaper.

**3. Finding 1 contradicts Section 1 and the figures.**
- Section 1 says late cancellations are reported separately from DNAs, and the 10.5% and £80,900 figures cover DNAs only (2,610 ÷ 24,860).
- Finding 1 says the 10.5% *includes* late cancellations, "which we classify as DNAs". That is wrong on both counts.
- If late cancellations were included, the figure would be (2,610 + 1,140) ÷ 24,860 = 15.1%, assuming those cancellations are within the 24,860 booked appointments. The memo should confirm this.
- The cost figure would also change, although refilled slots (31%) complicate it.

## Moderate issues

- **No projection supports the conclusion.** Reaching 8% requires about 620 fewer DNAs (from 2,610 to about 1,990). The memo never estimates how much each recommendation would contribute, so "should bring the DNA rate below target within six months" is an assertion.
- **The recommendations don't target where the problem is.** Follow-ups account for 2,200 of the 2,610 DNAs, and staff attribute this to patients quietly stopping once they feel better. Nothing addresses that, such as agreed treatment end-points, patient-initiated discharge, or a simple "cancel if you're better" message.
- **Recommendation 2 may not do what it claims.** Adding clinical review introduces more discretion, which may not make application more consistent. The memo should say how consistency will be monitored, since 104 of 160 (65%) were discharged. It also provides no evidence that discharge reduces DNAs.
- **Cost framing.** £80,900 assumes every slot is 30 minutes (new assessments may be longer) and treats lost time as recoverable cash. It is better described as capacity lost, not money saved.
- **Finding 3 has no benchmark.** It calls the 31% refill rate "only" 31% without a comparator or target. Recommendation 3 also lacks an expected improvement.

## Minor points

- Section 3 says "about 300 a week"; 7,800 ÷ 26 = 300, which is correct. The "about 960 a week" figure is also correct (24,860 ÷ 26 ≈ 956).
- Tables 1 and 2 sum correctly, and the rates are accurate to one decimal place.
- Interview evidence is cited, but the number of staff interviewed isn't given.

## Suggested fixes

1. Reword the reminder-call finding as an association, and note the selection effect. Better, recommend a pilot, such as calling all patients at one site or alternating weeks, and compare outcomes.
2. Add a workload and cost estimate for Recommendation 1, and remove "no additional cost" unless it can be shown.
3. Correct Finding 1 so it is consistent with Section 1, and report DNAs and late cancellations separately (10.5% and 4.6%, or 15.1% combined).
4. Add an expected-impact table for each recommendation against the 8% target.
5. Add a recommendation aimed at follow-up attendance.
